content.text: Which of the following describes the direction of the centripetal force acting on the satellite?
Same direction as the gravitational force
Opposite direction to the gravitational force
Same direction as the tangential velocity
Opposite direction to the tangential velocity

A satellite travelling along a circular path has a continuously changing velocity, so it must have a non-zero net force acting on it. Ask yourself which single force is available to act on the satellite, and towards which point it acts.

A centripetal force is not a separate force — it is the name given to whatever net force acts along the radius of the circular path, towards its centre. Use that definition to locate its direction in the diagram.
A

Gravity is the only force acting on the satellite and it always acts towards the centre of the Earth. A centripetal force is by definition the net force directed along the radius towards the centre of the circular path, so here it is in the same direction as the gravitational force. Option A.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - the centripetal force is in the same direction as the gravitational force

content.text: A spaceship sitting on its launch pad is measured to have a length $L$. This spaceship passes an outer planet at a speed of $0.95c$.
Which observations of the length of the spaceship are correct?
Observer on the spaceship: No change. Observer on the planet: Shorter than $L$.
Observer on the spaceship: No change. Observer on the planet: Greater than $L$.
Observer on the spaceship: Shorter than $L$. Observer on the planet: No change.
Observer on the spaceship: Greater than $L$. Observer on the planet: No change.
The length measured in the frame in which the spaceship is at rest is its proper length. That is the length quoted in the question, so decide which observer shares that frame.
For any observer who sees the spaceship moving, use $\ell = L\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$. Substitute $v = 0.95c$ and decide whether the factor you obtain is greater or less than 1.
A
$L$ is the proper length, measured in the rest frame of the spaceship, so observers on the spaceship measure no change.

The planet's observers see the spaceship moving, so they measure a length-contracted value $l = L\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$. At $v = 0.95c$ this is $L\sqrt{1 - 0.9025} = 0.31L$, which is shorter than $L$. Option A.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - no change for the spaceship's observers and shorter than $L$ for the planet's observers

content.text: The gravitational potential energy of a given mass is known at both Earth's surface and at a fixed distance above Earth.
What CANNOT be determined by comparing these two values of gravitational potential energy?
The mass of Earth
The speed of rotation of Earth
The escape velocity of a satellite from Earth
The work done in moving between the two points
Work through the first, third and fourth options in turn using $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ and $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, and see what each one would let you calculate from the two values of $U$.
Then ask which of the four listed quantities has no influence at all on Earth's gravitational field, so that it could leave no trace in any measurement of gravitational potential energy.
B
The difference in gravitational potential energy between the two points gives the work done in moving the mass between them, so D follows directly.

Since $U = -GMm/r$, comparing the two values at known separations allows $GM$, and hence the mass of Earth, to be found, so A follows; from that the escape velocity $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ follows, so C follows.
The rotation of Earth has no effect whatsoever on gravitational potential energy, so its speed of rotation cannot be deduced from these values. Option B.

items: 1 mark: selects option B - the speed of rotation of Earth

content.text: The acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface is $g$. Suppose the radius of Earth was reduced to a quarter of its present value while its mass remained the same.
What would be the new value of the acceleration due to gravity on the surface?
Write the field strength at the surface of a planet in terms of its mass and radius: $g = \frac{GM}{R^{2}}$.
Only the radius changes. Substitute $R_{new} = R/4$ and remember that the radius is squared in the denominator.
D
$g = GM/R^{2}$. With the mass unchanged and the radius reduced to $R/4$, the new value is $GM/(R/4)^{2} = 16GM/R^{2} = 16g$. Option D.

content.text: A cannon ball is fired vertically upward from a stationary boat.
Which pair of graphs best describes the velocity, $v$, and acceleration, $a$, of the cannon ball as functions of time, $t$? Ignore air resistance.

content.alt_text: Pair of graphs. The $v$ against $t$ graph shows a straight line rising from zero to a peak then falling linearly back to zero. The $a$ against $t$ graph shows a positive constant value, a sudden step down through zero, then a negative constant value.
Pair of graphs. The $v$ against $t$ graph shows a straight line falling from a positive value to zero then rising again. The $a$ against $t$ graph shows a single negative constant value.

Pair of graphs. The $v$ against $t$ graph shows a straight line falling from positive through zero to negative. The $a$ against $t$ graph shows a straight line rising from negative through zero to positive.

Pair of graphs. The $v$ against $t$ graph shows a straight line falling from a positive value through zero to a negative value. The $a$ against $t$ graph shows a single negative constant value below the time axis.

content.text: Once the ball has left the boat, list the vertical forces acting on it. Since an object can only accelerate in response to a net force, this alone fixes the shape of the $a$ against $t$ graph.
Then obtain the $v$ against $t$ graph from $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$: the gradient is constant, so follow $v$ through zero at the top of the flight and keep going as the ball falls.
D

Once the ball leaves the boat the only vertical force acting on it is gravity, so the acceleration is constant at $-g$ for the whole flight. This rules out A and C, whose acceleration graphs are not constant.

The velocity starts at a positive value and decreases uniformly at $g$, passing through zero at the top of the trajectory and becoming negative on the way down. This is the $v$ graph in D, which is paired with the constant negative $a$ graph, so D is correct. B is wrong because its $v$ graph turns back upwards, which cannot happen under constant gravity.

items: 1 mark: selects option D - velocity decreasing uniformly through zero with a constant negative acceleration

content.text: When current is supplied the coil does not turn.
Which of the following is required for the coil to start turning?
The magnetic field must be increased.
The direction of the current must be reversed.
The magnitude of the current must be increased.
The starting position of the coil must be changed.
Consider the torque on the coil, $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the field and the normal to the plane of the coil.

Look at the diagram and decide where the plane of the coil sits relative to the field, then ask what the forces on the two sides of the coil do to one another. Will changing the size of $B$ or $I$ alter that geometric conclusion?
D

The torque on the coil is $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$, so it is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field ($\theta = 90^\circ$) and is zero when the coil lies in the neutral plane with the field normal to its plane.
As drawn, the coil sits in the neutral plane, so the forces on its two sides are equal and opposite and produce no net turning effect.
Increasing $B$ or $I$, or reversing the current, does not change this: the torque is still zero. The coil must be displaced from the neutral plane so that a net torque acts. Option D.

content.text: Which modification was made to produce the result shown?
The area of the coil was doubled.
A split-ring commutator was added.
The speed of rotation of the coil was doubled.
The number of turns in the coil was quadrupled.
For a rotating coil, $|\varepsilon|_{\max} = NBA\omega$, and the frequency of the output emf is also proportional to $\omega$.

Read the peak amplitude and the number of cycles completed in a fixed time interval off each curve and compare them. Then ask which of the four modifications would change the frequency as well as the amplitude, and which would change only the amplitude.
C
$|\varepsilon| = BA\omega$, so the peak emf is directly proportional to the rotation speed $\omega$, and the frequency of the emf is also $\omega$.
The dashed curve has twice the amplitude and twice the frequency of the solid curve, so the rotation speed was doubled. Option C.

Doubling the area (A) or quadrupling the turns (D) would change the amplitude but leave the frequency unchanged. A split-ring commutator (B) would rectify the output so that it became a series of positive pulses, which is not what the dashed curve shows.

content.text: Which graph best represents the corresponding induced emf in the coil?

content.alt_text: Graph of induced emf against time showing a smooth sinusoidal curve that starts at zero, peaks positive, crosses zero, troughs negative and repeats.
Graph of induced emf against time showing a smooth sinusoidal curve that starts at zero, dips negative, crosses zero, peaks positive, dips negative and returns to zero.
Graph of induced emf against time showing a square wave that starts at a positive level, drops to a negative level, rises to a positive level and drops to a negative level again.
Graph of induced emf against time showing a square wave that starts at a negative level, rises to a positive level, drops to a negative level and rises to a positive level again.

content.text: The induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux, $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$, so read the gradient of the flux graph rather than its height.

Decide whether that gradient is constant, and then use Lenz's law to fix the sign: the induced emf opposes the change in flux, so begin by asking whether the flux is increasing or decreasing as the printed graph starts.
D

The flux changes linearly within each segment of the triangular waveform, so $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ is constant in each segment and the magnitude of the induced emf $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$ is constant. The emf is therefore a square wave, not a sine wave, which rules out A and B.
The sign of the emf opposes the sign of the flux change, so the emf is negative wherever the flux is increasing and positive wherever the flux is decreasing.
The printed flux graph starts by increasing from zero, so the emf must start negative, which rules out option C (which starts positive) and leaves option D.

content.text: A stationary exercise bike has a solid metal wheel that is rotated by a chain connected to the pedals. An array of strong permanent magnets provides a magnetic field close to the face of the wheel.
The exercise level can be selected from 1 (easy) to 6 (hard) using a control panel.
When level 6 is selected, which of the following statements is correct?
The current supplied to the bike is a minimum.
The magnetic field at the wheel is a minimum.
The induced current in the wheel is a maximum.
The distance between the magnets and the wheel is a maximum.
A harder setting has to make the wheel harder to turn. Think about what the control panel can change in order to increase the resistive drag the rider feels.

Use $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$ for the current induced in the metal wheel: identify what the control does to $B$ and to the gap between magnet and wheel, and hence what it does to the induced current and to the power dissipated as heat.
C
At the hardest setting the magnets are brought closer to the wheel, giving a larger rate of change of magnetic flux through the metal of the wheel.
The magnitude of the induced eddy current, $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$, is then at a maximum, and the larger electromagnetic drag means more pedal effort is needed.
Options A, B and D all describe conditions that would reduce the induced current, which is the opposite of what a hard setting requires. Option C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - the induced current in the wheel is a maximum

content.text: What is the wave property that enabled Hertz to calculate the velocity of radiowaves and compare it to the velocity of light?
Interference
Polarisation
Reflection
Refraction

Hertz needed to measure the wavelength of his radiowaves, not merely to detect them. Which wave behaviour allows a wavelength to be measured from the positions of nodes or of reinforced and cancelled signals?

He used a spark-gap transmitter and a small loop with a gap as the receiver. Think about how arranging these two at distances that are whole numbers of wavelengths apart would let the node spacing be measured.
A
Hertz used a spark-gap transmitter and detected the radiowaves with a small loop containing a gap that sparked when the voltage across it was high enough.

He arranged the transmitter and receiver at distances that were whole numbers of wavelengths, so that the direct wave and the reflected wave arrived in phase and reinforced one another. This standing-wave interference allowed the node spacing to be measured and hence the wavelength to be found.

Combining the wavelength with the known frequency gave the wave velocity, which agreed with the speed of light. Polarisation, reflection and refraction on their own provide no way of measuring the wavelength. Option A.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - interference

content.text: The Bragg experiment used X-rays to investigate crystal structure.
Which statement best describes the results of this experiment?
X-rays are scattered from a crystal and form an interference pattern.
X-rays penetrate a crystal and form an interference pattern behind it.
X-rays are absorbed and re-emitted equally in all directions by a crystal.
X-rays absorbed by a crystal produce minima and those reflected produce maxima.

Waves scattered from atoms in successive planes of a crystal travel different distances, so they interfere. Maxima then appear only at particular angles of incidence, giving $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$.

Decide whether the pattern is built from waves that pass through the crystal unchanged, or from waves that are scattered (reflected) back out of the crystal planes. Absorption followed by re-emission in all directions would produce no pattern at all.
A
X-rays were incident at various angles on the faces of a crystal. Waves scattered from atoms in successive crystal planes travel different distances, so they interfere.

Constructive interference occurs only at particular angles of incidence, producing a pattern of intensity maxima from which both the wavelength and the plane spacing could be determined - the Bragg equation $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$.

The X-rays are therefore scattered or reflected from the crystal planes. They do not simply pass through the crystal to form the pattern behind it (B), they are not absorbed and re-emitted in all directions (C), and there is no division of the beam into separate 'absorbed' and 'reflected' bands (D). Option A.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - X-rays are scattered from a crystal and form an interference pattern

content.text: An electron is moving near a long straight wire. When a current is applied to the wire the electron experiences a force in the same direction as the current flow in the wire.
What was the electron's initial direction of motion?
Parallel to the current direction
Opposite to the current direction
Towards the wire and perpendicular to it
Away from the wire and perpendicular to it
The current in the wire produces a magnetic field that circles the wire. Use the right-hand grip rule to find which way that field points at the position of the electron.

The force is $F = qvB\sin\theta$ and the electron is negatively charged, so the force acts opposite to $\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$. Note too that a velocity along or against the current is parallel to $\mathbf{B}$ and would give zero force.
C

The current in the wire produces a circular magnetic field around the wire. The force on the electron is $F = qvB\sin\theta$, which is zero if the velocity is parallel to $B$, so a velocity along or against the current (options A and B) could not produce any force at all.

Take the current along $+z$ and consider an electron on the $+x$ side of the wire, where the field is along $-y$. For the magnetic force on the electron to be along $+z$ (the current direction) we need $\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$ along $-z$, which requires $\mathbf{v}$ along $-x$: the electron moves towards the wire, perpendicular to the current. Option C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - towards the wire and perpendicular to it

content.text: Which of the following is a property of a silicon $p$-type semiconductor?
It is positively charged.
It has fewer holes than pure silicon.
It can be produced by doping the silicon with boron.
It can be produced by doping the silicon with phosphorus.
Compare the number of valence electrons in silicon (group 14) with the number in each of the two doping elements named in the options.

A dopant with one fewer valence electron leaves vacancies, called holes, in the lattice and produces $p$-type material; a dopant with one extra produces $n$-type. Also recall that doping changes the carrier density, not the overall electrical neutrality of the sample.
C
A $p$-type semiconductor is made by doping silicon with a group 13 element such as boron, which has one fewer valence electron than silicon.
Each boron atom in the lattice leaves a vacancy, or hole, so the doped material has more holes than pure silicon; B is therefore wrong.

The material remains electrically neutral overall, so it is not positively charged, which rules out A. Doping with a group 15 element such as phosphorus produces an $n$-type semiconductor, ruling out D. Option C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - it can be produced by doping the silicon with boron

content.text: What CANNOT be calculated using the principle of conservation of energy?
The energy of a proton at rest
The production of back emf in a motor
Voltage transformation in an ideal transformer
The escape velocity of an object from the gravitational field of a planet

Take options B, C and D one at a time and write the energy balance that each relies on: for the motor, where does the back emf come from; for the transformer, what fixes $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$; for escape velocity, what is the total energy at infinite distance?
Then ask which of the four requires a separate principle relating mass to energy, rather than a balance of energy between a starting and a final state.
A
The back emf in a motor follows from conservation of energy, since electrical energy is converted into kinetic and thermal energy, so B does follow from conservation of energy.
In an ideal transformer $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$ is a direct statement of the conservation of energy, so C follows.
The escape velocity follows by setting the total mechanical energy of the object at infinity equal to zero, so D follows.
The rest energy of a proton requires the mass-energy equivalence $E = mc^{2}$, which comes from the special theory of relativity and is a separate principle, not conservation of energy. Option A.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - the energy of a proton at rest

content.text: How has our understanding of time been influenced by the discovery of the constancy of the speed of light?

The marking guide credits any one of three things, so pick the one you can argue properly instead of touching all three: the relativity of time, using $c$ to define length, or a concrete example of a moving clock running slow.
Whichever you choose, tie it explicitly to $c$ having the same value for every observer. That single statement is what forces time and length to be attached to a frame of reference.
Because every observer measures the same value of $c$, time and length are only meaningful relative to a frame of reference; a moving clock is measured to run slow (time dilation).
Einstein's second postulate states that the speed of light in a vacuum has the same value $c$ for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.

Since every observer measures the same $c$ for the same light pulse, and $t = d/c$, any observer who measures the same path length $d$ for that pulse must measure the same elapsed time. Time and length are therefore only meaningful relative to a frame of reference.
For a rapidly moving object the measured interval is dilated, $t = t_0/\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$, so a clock carried by the object runs slow relative to the observer's clock. Time is not absolute.

content.text: Analyse Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity and the evidence supporting it as an application of this model of scientific method.

Walk the flowchart one box at a time and label your paragraphs with the box you are dealing with — observation, problem raised, new hypothesis, experiment to test, collection of data, analysis of results, support — so that no step in the model is missed.

The observation and problem-raised boxes come from classical physics failing: the Michelson–Morley null result and the way the speed of light behaved in different frames of reference. The new-hypothesis box is Einstein's two postulates.

For the experiment and data boxes, use the tests that were actually carried out — muon lifetimes measured in the laboratory and in the atmosphere, and atomic clocks flown on aircraft compared with clocks left on the ground — then check the analysis against the time-dilation relationship.

Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity is the hypothesis; time dilation of muons and of atomic clocks, and the Michelson-Morley result, are the supporting evidence; the theory has been accepted because the evidence consistently supports it.
Observation: the Michelson-Morley experiment detected no expected 'ether wind', and measurements of the speed of light from different frames did not agree with classical prediction.
Problem raised: classical (Newtonian) physics assumed an absolute frame of reference and could not account for these observations.
New hypothesis: Einstein proposed that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers and that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.

Experiment to test hypothesis and collection of data: muon lifetimes measured in laboratories and in the atmosphere, 'twin paradox' journeys, and comparison of atomic clocks flown on aircraft with clocks left on the ground.
Analysis of results: the observed time dilations agree with the predictions of $t = t_0/\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$ and the data do not depend on the frame of reference.

Support for hypothesis: the experimental evidence strongly supports the theory, which has been accepted and now underpins modern physics. Where the original theory did not explain everything, it was revised and extended rather than discarded.

content.text: Assess the effects of the development of AC generators on today's society and the environment.
The decisive feature of AC for a distribution system is that its voltage can be changed with a transformer, so begin by linking step-up and step-down to transmission efficiency.

Then turn that into impacts. Trace what cheap, reliable electricity actually made possible in homes, industry and commerce, and identify something that DC could not have supported over long distances.

The question names both society and the environment, so argue the environmental effects (generation from fossil fuels, and the land and habitat disrupted by lines and substations) rather than merely listing them, before you make your value judgement.

AC generators have enabled cheap, reliable electricity to be generated and transmitted over long distances and used in homes, industry and commerce, at the cost of greenhouse gas emissions from fossil-fuel power stations and landscape disruption from power lines.

Positive effects on society: AC can be stepped up to very high voltages for efficient long-distance transmission, so electricity reaches cities, homes and rural areas. AC powers appliances, industrial machinery, computers and communication, raising living standards and supporting modern economies.

Negative effects on the environment: most electricity is still generated by burning fossil fuels, releasing carbon dioxide and contributing to climate change. Power lines and substations occupy and fragment land and habitats, and large hydro schemes disturb river systems, while mining and manufacturing of generators and cables cause their own pollution.

A value judgement: on balance the development of AC generation has greatly improved human life, but the environmental cost is significant and is now being addressed by more efficient generators, better transmission and a shift to renewable sources.

content.text: Explain why solid state devices have largely replaced thermionic devices.
Begin by identifying what the two devices have in common — they perform the same job in a circuit — and then describe in one or two lines how each of them does it.

The thermionic device needs a heated filament, an evacuated envelope and a heater supply. List the practical consequences of those three requirements for size, power consumption, fragility and operating lifetime.

Do the same for the solid state device, then turn the comparison into the reason for replacement: which of the problems forced on you by the valve simply disappear, and which of its advantages does the solid state device gain.
Solid state devices are smaller, cheaper, more reliable, use far less power and have no warm-up time, whereas thermionic devices are bulky, fragile, run hot and consume much more power.
Both types of device perform a similar function: they control or switch a current in a circuit in response to a small electrical input.

A thermionic device, such as a thermionic valve, works by heating a cathode so that electrons are emitted from its surface; it must be evacuated and housed in a glass envelope and needs heater supplies.
A solid state device, such as a transistor or integrated circuit, works by the movement of carriers in a doped semiconductor; it needs no heated cathode, no vacuum envelope and no heater supply.

Solid state devices are therefore much smaller, lighter, cheaper, more robust, switch faster, have no warm-up time and consume a tiny fraction of the power of thermionic devices, which is why they have largely replaced them.

To develop materials with a critical temperature as close to, and preferably above, room temperature.
$T_c$ has risen from 16 K in 1941 to 92 K in 1987 and 133 K in 1993, so the trend is towards a higher critical temperature.
A material that becomes superconducting at or above about 273 K (room temperature) could be used without costly cooling, so that is what scientists are trying to achieve.

content.text: Describe what happens to one property of superconductors near the critical temperature.
Only one property is required, but it has to be paired with what happens to that property as the temperature approaches $T_c$ from above. A property named with no change attached earns nothing.
Electrical resistance is the most obvious choice, but the expulsion of magnetic flux below $T_c$ and the anomaly in heat capacity are also acceptable provided the change is described.
The electrical resistance falls to zero as the temperature approaches the critical temperature from above.
Above $T_c$ the material has a small but non-zero resistance and shows no Meissner effect.

As the temperature falls to $T_c$ the resistance drops rapidly and then becomes exactly zero below $T_c$. The material also expels magnetic flux (the Meissner effect) and its heat capacity shows an anomaly.

content.text: Explain why magnetic levitation occurs in superconducting materials.

Two ideas carry the whole explanation and they must appear in this order: a superconductor below its critical temperature expels magnetic field from its interior, and an induced current always opposes a change in magnetic flux.

Follow the sequence through — magnet approaches, flux through the superconductor would change, induced currents oppose that change, the currents produce a field that repels the magnet — and the levitation explains itself without any additional mechanism.
A superconductor below its critical temperature expels magnetic flux, so a magnet brought near it is repelled and levitates.
Below $T_c$ a superconductor expels magnetic field from its interior, the Meissner effect, so the magnetic flux threading it cannot change.
As a magnet is brought towards a superconductor the flux threading it would change, so an induced current is set up that opposes the change in flux (Lenz's law).
The field produced by this induced current opposes the magnet's field, giving a repulsive force that supports the magnet against gravity, so it levitates.

content.text: A student claims that a DC generator is an 'electric motor in reverse'.
Analyse this claim with reference to the structure and function of a simple DC generator and an electric motor.
Include diagrams in your answer.
Draw the two devices first, side by side, labelling the components they share and the components that differ. A large share of the marks are earned in these labelled diagrams alone.

For each device, name the energy going in and the energy coming out, and identify the effect responsible — the motor effect in one, electromagnetic induction in the other — together with the component that performs the switching.

Then judge the claim in two parts: is the student right about the structure, and is the student right about what the devices do? Use your energy comparison to support the second part of the judgement.

The claim is partly correct: the same basic components (a coil between field magnets, a split-ring commutator and brushes) are used, but a DC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy while a motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
A simple DC motor and a simple DC generator contain the same common components: a coil (rotor or armature) rotating on an axis between field magnets, a split-ring commutator, and carbon brushes.

In a motor an external voltage drives a current through the coil. The resulting force on the conductors, $F = BIl\sin\theta$, produces a torque, $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$, that turns the coil, so electrical energy is converted into kinetic energy and some into thermal energy in the resistance of the coil.

In a DC generator the coil is turned mechanically, so it cuts magnetic flux. By electromagnetic induction $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$, and the split-ring commutator rectifies the induced emf so that direct current flows out through the brushes, so mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.

The claim is therefore correct about the structure, which is why a DC generator and a DC motor are physically very similar, but it is not correct about the direction of energy conversion: the two devices convert energy in opposite directions.

content.text: Explain why AC is preferable to DC as an input current for transformers.
The marking guide gives the full mark only if the explanation is in terms of a change in magnetic flux, so build the answer around flux rather than around currents or electrons.
Ask what a steady DC current does to the flux in the primary coil, then what follows for the secondary coil when that flux does not change.
A transformer needs a changing magnetic flux in the primary coil, and only an alternating current produces a continuously changing flux, which in turn induces an emf in the secondary coil.
A steady DC current produces a steady magnetic field in the primary coil, so there is no change in magnetic flux and hence no induced emf in the secondary coil: transformers do not work with DC.

An alternating current produces a magnetic flux in the primary coil that is continuously changing, and this changing flux links the secondary coil, inducing an alternating emf that can then be stepped up or stepped down.

content.text: Outline possible causes of energy loss in the transformer.

Resistive heating in the windings, eddy currents induced in the core, and flux that does not link the secondary coil.
The primary and secondary windings are copper, which has resistance, so some electrical energy is converted to thermal energy as the current flows ($P = I^2R$).
A changing magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the iron core, and these produce thermal energy and an opposing field.
Some of the primary flux does not link the secondary coil, so not all the energy is transferred.
Hysteresis in the core also converts some energy to thermal energy as the magnetisation is reversed each cycle.

content.text: Scientists tried to explain observations of black-body radiation using classical wave theory and then quantum theory.
How does quantum theory satisfactorily explain black-body radiation?

The full mark needs two halves joined together: describe the black body and the shape of its radiation curve, then link that shape to energy being emitted in packets. Answering only one half caps the mark at two.

Make the failure of the classical account explicit, because that is what quantum theory has to explain. Say what classical theory predicted at the short-wavelength end of the spectrum and what is actually observed there.
The mechanism worth stating is that at high frequency the energy quantum is large, so very few oscillators in the body can be excited and little energy is radiated at short wavelengths.

A black body absorbs all radiation incident on it and emits a continuous spectrum whose peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as its temperature rises; quantum theory explains the shape because the energy is emitted in discrete quanta of size $E = hf$, so the short-wavelength high-energy tail predicted by classical theory is not produced.

A theoretical black body is a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter of radiation at all wavelengths, and it emits a continuous spectrum with a characteristic shape whose peak moves to shorter wavelengths as the temperature increases.

Classical wave theory cannot explain this shape. Applying the equipartition idea to the oscillators predicts that the short-wavelength end of the spectrum becomes very intense, the 'ultraviolet catastrophe', which is not observed.

Quantum theory states that the oscillators in the body can have only energies that are integer multiples of $hf$, where $h$ is Planck's constant and $f$ the frequency. At high frequencies the energy quantum $hf$ is large, so very few oscillators can be excited and little energy is radiated at short wavelengths.
The resulting curve peaks at a wavelength $\lambda_{max}$ that moves to shorter wavelengths as $T$ increases, exactly as observed.

content.text: Describe Hertz's observation of the photoelectric effect.

Hertz shone ultraviolet light onto a zinc surface in a vacuum and observed a small spark at the receiving loop, showing that ultraviolet light could produce an electric current in a metal.
Hertz used his spark-gap transmitter to produce ultraviolet light and directed it onto a polished zinc plate in an evacuated gap.
He observed a small spark at the receiving loop whenever ultraviolet light fell on the zinc, showing that electrons were emitted from the metal and travelled across the gap to produce the spark.
He also found that the effect occurred only for ultraviolet light, not for light of longer wavelength.

content.text: A gradient needs two points well separated on the same straight line, so use the point where the sodium line crosses the frequency axis and a second point near the top of that line. Write down both pairs of values before you subtract.

Keep the axis units in the answer. The horizontal axis is in units of $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and a gradient quoted per $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ converts directly into electron-volts per second, which is Planck's constant in the units the graph uses.
For the second part, ask what a gradient that is identical for four different metals cannot be. If it were a property of the metals it would have to differ between them, so where does that leave it?

(i) Gradient $\approx 3.9\,\mathrm{eV}$ per $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, i.e. about $3.9 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eV\,s}$, which is Planck's constant (accepted value $4.14 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eV\,s}$). (ii) The gradient is the same for every metal, so it is a property of light and not of the material; it must be Planck's constant, and only the threshold frequency, where each line crosses the frequency axis, carries information about the metal.

The sodium line crosses the frequency axis at its threshold frequency, about $0.6 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, where the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is zero because the photons are just supplying the work function and no more. A second point is taken near the top right of the same line, about $7.1\,\mathrm{eV}$ at $2.4 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$:

In seconds rather than units of $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ that is about $3.9 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eV\,s}$, which agrees with the accepted value of Planck's constant to within the reading accuracy of the graph. Any value in the range $3.9$ to $4.2\,\mathrm{eV}$ per $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ should be accepted from this graph.

The significance of the parallel lines is the point of the second part. From Einstein's photoelectric equation $K_{\max} = hf - \phi$ the gradient is $h$ for every material, and the work function $\phi$ only sets where the line crosses the frequency axis. Four metals giving four different threshold frequencies but one common gradient therefore shows that the constant is a property of light itself, independent of the metal, which is strong evidence for the quantum model. If the gradient were a property of the metal it would have to be different for each of the four.

Whatever survey is being described, its corrections exist to remove the known effects of position and height so that what is left over is a property of the ground itself.
Work each station separately and write the three corrections in the order latitude, free air, Bouguer, keeping track of which height each one uses.
Then ask what the size and the sign of the remaining anomaly implies about the density of the rock beneath each station, compared with the density the corrections assumed.
Part

. The graph referred to in the question plots the speeds of P and S waves against depth, but in the 2007 paper that figure is printed only as an 'Awaiting copyright' placeholder and is not attached, so the comparison has to be made from the physical model of the interior.

An S wave is transverse: it displaces the medium perpendicular to its own direction of travel, so it can only propagate through a medium with a non-zero rigidity. The liquid outer core has no rigidity, so the S-wave velocity drops to zero there, and the S-wave curve is the direct experimental evidence that the outer core is liquid. The mantle above it and the solid inner core below it both support shear stress, so S waves pass through both, and they travel fastest in the inner core, where both rigidity and density are greatest.

A P wave is longitudinal, so it travels through solids and liquids alike and appears at every depth. Its speed depends on the elastic properties of the medium, increasing with rigidity and with density, so the P-wave curve rises steadily with depth through the mantle and shows sharp jumps at the core-mantle boundary and at the inner-core boundary, where the material changes abruptly, with a marked reduction as the rays approach the liquid outer core.

Explain how these south magnetic pole positions were determined and how they provide evidence for continental drift. (4 marks)

** When iron-rich lava cooled, the iron grains in it aligned with Earth's magnetic field at that moment and that direction was locked into the rock as it solidified. This palaeomagnetism can be measured in each continent, and because rocks of a given age record the same field direction, the direction of the field at the time can be recovered and extrapolated to give the position of the south magnetic pole as seen from that continent. When the five apparent pole positions are plotted on one map they coincide, close to the centre of Antarctica, instead of lying far apart as they would if each continent had always been where it is now. There was only one south magnetic pole, so the coincidence can only be explained by the continents having once been joined and having since drifted apart, which is direct evidence for continental drift.

. Lava is rich in iron, and as it solidifies the iron grains align with the Earth's field at the time of cooling and are locked into the rock. Heating a sample in a laboratory re-sets that alignment, so the ancient field direction can be read from the rock. Rocks of the same age in different continents record the same field direction, so the apparent pole position can be calculated for each continent from its own rocks and its own present position. Plotting all five apparent positions on a single map shows them coinciding rather than spread out, which is what would happen if each continent had always been where it is today. Because there was only one south magnetic pole, that coincidence is evidence that the continents were once joined and have since moved apart.

content.text: Remote sensing by satellites has added greatly to our ability to understand Earth.
Analyse how the introduction of satellites has contributed to TWO areas of knowledge of Earth that were previously inaccessible.

Choose two areas and give each its own paragraph. In each paragraph make three things explicit: what could not be done before, what the satellite measures, and how that measurement changed the area of knowledge.

The marking notes require the previously inaccessible feature to be named, not implied. Say precisely what no ground-based instrument could do — a single satellite in orbit can see a whole hemisphere at once.
Close by contrasting the satellite record with the old local, spot measurement. That contrast is what makes the relationship between the technology and the new knowledge evident.

Satellites have made global knowledge possible in areas such as weather forecasting and climate monitoring, via passive microwave and infrared sensing, and in geological and mineral exploration, via remote sensing of the surface at many wavelengths and radar altimetry.

Area 1 - meteorology and climate: satellites in orbit observe the whole Earth continuously, measuring outgoing microwave radiation from the oceans, infrared radiation from the surface and visible reflected light. This gives global coverage of cloud, rainfall, sea surface temperature, wind and ice extent, so weather forecasts are far more accurate and long-term climate change can be tracked. This was previously inaccessible because no ground-based instrument can observe the whole globe at once.

Area 2 - geology and mineral exploration: satellites carry sensors that detect the surface at many wavelengths, including radar that penetrates dry sand and vegetation. Differences in the returned radiation reveal the type and structure of rocks, faults, folds and the surface expression of ore bodies, so large areas can be mapped quickly and cheaply, including remote, rugged and densely vegetated regions that could not be surveyed on foot.

Satellites have also made inaccessible areas accessible: the poles, the deep ocean floor, the atmosphere at all altitudes and the far side of the Moon have all been studied for the first time from orbit.
Overall, satellite remote sensing has transformed Earth science by replacing local, indirect, spot measurements with global, direct, repeated measurements.

content.alt_text: Two seismic traces drawn one above the other. The upper trace, labelled Nuclear test, shows a single sharp initial pulse followed by a small, rapidly decaying series of oscillations. The lower trace, labelled Earthquake, shows a much longer trace with a small initial arrival followed by a large, sustained and slowly decaying series of oscillations. A caption reads 'Ack: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory'.

content.text: Compare the traces feature by feature: onset sharpness, peak amplitude, total duration of the wave train, and how quickly the amplitude decays.
Then ask what the source must have been doing to produce each trace. Duration of the train is set by how long the source radiates energy, not by how far the waves travel.
For locating and identifying the source, remember that two wave types are recorded, and that the interval between their arrivals depends on distance but not on when the event happened.

items: (d)(i) The two traces differ in every respect that matters. The nuclear-test trace has a single sharp, abrupt onset followed by a relatively small train of oscillations that dies away within a few seconds; there is no gradual build-up. The earthquake trace has a small initial arrival followed by a much larger wave train that persists for many tens of seconds and decays slowly. The explanation is the nature of the two sources. A nuclear test is a single impulsive event confined to a small volume at a shallow depth: all the energy is released within a fraction of a second from a source of limited extent, so the onset is abrupt, the high-frequency content is large because the energy is released near the surface, and the amplitude decays quickly as the small source ceases to radiate and the energy spreads away from the sensor. An earthquake, by contrast, is a rupture that propagates along a fault plane for a length of perhaps tens of kilometres and continues for minutes, so the source is effectively a moving line source that pumps energy into the rock throughout that time. That is why the earthquake train builds to a much larger amplitude and decays slowly, and why the total energy, and hence the magnitude, is very much greater.

(d)(ii) A seismogram is used in two ways. To locate the source, the P-wave and S-wave arrivals are read off the trace and their interval $\Delta t = t_S - t_P$ is measured; since $\Delta t$ depends only on the distance from the epicentre (about $8.5\,\mathrm{km}$ per degree), each station defines a circle, and the intersection of the circles from three or more stations fixes the epicentre without needing to know the origin time. The distance and the depth then give the magnitude from the recorded amplitude, so the same trace yields location and size. To identify the source, the shape of the trace is itself diagnostic: a small, impulsive onset with strong high-frequency content and rapid decay, at a shallow focal depth and with a large ratio of S-wave to P-wave amplitude in some circumstances, matches an explosive source, whereas a long, large, slowly decaying train with an emergent onset matches a tectonic rupture. This is why seismologists can distinguish a nuclear test from an earthquake on a single record, and why the distinctive shallow-focus signature of a test is the basis of the monitoring that arms-control treaties require.

content.text: Reading the traces. Measure the same four features on each: the time to the first arrival, whether the onset is abrupt or gradual, the peak amplitude, and the time over which the oscillations remain significant. The test trace gives an abrupt onset with a short, small, rapidly decaying train; the earthquake trace gives a small initial arrival then a large, sustained, slowly decaying train. The total amplitude is not a reliable measure of the source energy on its own, because it also depends on distance, so the comparison is made at similar distances and stations.

Explaining the difference through the source. A seismogram is the convolution of the source time function with the propagation path and the instrument response. A nuclear test is effectively a single impulse: the source time function is a spike of duration well under a second, which produces an abrupt onset and a broadband pulse dominated by high frequencies, and because the source is small and shallow the radiation is focused upward along the ray path, so the train dies away quickly as the energy spreads. An earthquake is a rupture of up to hundreds of kilometres over minutes: the source time function is a long, large signal, so the trace rises to a much greater amplitude and stays large for as long as the rupture continues. The decay of the earthquake train after the rupture stops is controlled by scattering and anelastic attenuation through kilometres of rock, which is why it is gradual.

content.text: Ultrasound imaging depends on the fact that different materials have different acoustic impedances. The density and acoustic impedance of fat and muscle are shown.

content.alt_text: Table with columns 'Density (kg m^-3)' and 'Acoustic impedance (kg m^-2 s^-1 x 10^6)'. Fat: 9.25 x 10^2, 1.38. Muscle: 1.073 x 10^3, 1.70.

content.text: The speed is not given in the table: it is the impedance divided by the density, and doing this for both tissues also gives you the ratio of the speeds.
For the boundary between the two tissues, use the reflection coefficients. Work out the amplitude coefficient first, then remember that the fraction of intensity reflected is its square.

Then ask the imaging question: an ultrasound image is built from returning echoes, so any interface that reflects part of the pulse draws a line on the image. Fat and muscle are exactly such an interface.

items: (a)(i) Speeds of sound from $v = Z/\rho$. In fat: $\dfrac{1.38 \times 10^{6}}{9.25 \times 10^{2}} = 1.49 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. In muscle: $\dfrac{1.70 \times 10^{6}}{1.073 \times 10^{3}} = 1.58 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The sound therefore travels about $6\,\%$ faster in muscle than in fat, and both speeds are close to $1.5\,\mathrm{km/s}$, which is the standard value assumed for soft tissue.

(a)(ii) Reflection at the fat-muscle interface. Amplitude coefficient $r = \dfrac{1.70 - 1.38}{1.70 + 1.38} = \dfrac{0.32}{3.08} = 0.104$, so the fraction of intensity reflected is $r^{2} = 0.0108$, i.e. $1.1\,$%, and $98.9\,$% is transmitted into the muscle. Two consequences follow. First, every boundary between tissues of different impedance produces a returning echo, and it is the time of return (one half of the round trip divided by the local speed) that sets the position of that boundary on the scan, so the fat-muscle interface, being the closest of these interfaces to the probe, is drawn as a bright line separating the two. Second, because fat is the least dense and lowest-impedance common tissue and muscle is markedly higher, the mismatch at this particular interface is larger than at most others: a small fraction of the transmitted energy is enough to form a clear echo, which is why fat, and in particular the layer of fat over muscle, is the boundary most easily resolved and why the eye and the soft tissue around it are examined well by ultrasound. Because the reflected fraction is small, most of the energy continues into the deeper tissue, which is why several layers can be imaged with a single scan.

content.text: Part (i). Acoustic impedance is $Z = \rho v$, so $v = Z/\rho$.
Both values are of the expected order for soft tissue, which is the check that the tabulated impedances carry the $\times 10^{6}$ multiplier shown in the table header.

Part (ii). The amplitude reflection coefficient is $0.104$ and the intensity reflection coefficient is $1.1\,\%$, so $98.9\,\%$ of the pulse passes on into the muscle. The image is built from these returning echoes: the time of arrival of an echo is determined by the distance the pulse travelled down and back and the local speed, so the fat-muscle boundary, the first strong reflector encountered in most examinations, produces the first bright line in the scan and marks the depth of the underlying muscle. This is the physics behind the standard use of ultrasound to image the eye, the neck, the breast and the abdomen, where the fat layer overlying muscle provides the first landmark and the contrast between them is large enough to be seen clearly.

content.text: In your study of Medical Physics you performed an investigation to identify the function of the components of MRI equipment. The following information is from the Australian Twin Registry Newsletter, 2006.
MRI: How does it work?

Unlike conventional radiography Computed Tomography (CT) scans, which make use of potentially harmful X-rays passing through a patient to generate images, MRI is based on the magnetic properties of atoms within the tissue. A powerful magnet generates a magnetic field roughly 10,000 times stronger than the Earth's. A very small percentage of hydrogen atoms within the body will line up with this field. Radio waves are passed through the person's body then "bounce back" depending on how many lined up atoms they meet. The subtle differences in how the radio waves bounce back provide the information needed to construct the image.
Australian Twin Registry
Assess the information provided in this article in terms of its scientific accuracy.
Part (i) is about mechanism at the level of atoms: start from what happens when a photon interacts with matter, and follow it through to the outcome for the cell.
Dose is measured in gray, and the biological effect also depends on the radiation type; make sure you distinguish energy absorbed per unit mass from the amount of energy in the beam.

For part (ii), think about how the tumour can be spared: shaping the beam, choosing a source whose energy is deposited over the right depth, and exploiting the fact that healthy cells can repair between doses but a tumour cannot keep up.

The article is a broadly correct lay summary, but two of its statements are inaccurate. Correct: MRI is based on the magnetic properties of atoms in the tissue - it uses the magnetic moment of the nuclei of hydrogen (protons) in the water and fat of the body - and a very small fraction of those nuclei do line up with the field (at body temperature only about 1 in $10^{7}$ are in the lower-energy aligned state). Inaccurate: the magnet is much stronger than 'roughly 10,000 times Earth's field', since a clinical unit of $1.5$ to $3\,\mathrm{T}$ is some 30 000 to 60 000 times Earth's field of about $50\,\mu\mathrm{T}$; and the radio waves do not 'bounce back' off the lined-up atoms - the applied radiofrequency pulse tips the magnetisation over and the signal is the radiofrequency radiation emitted as the precessing protons relax, so the image depends on the density and chemical environment of the hydrogen nuclei, not on the number of atoms a wave 'meets'. Judgement: the outline is accurate enough for a general reader, but the field strength is wrong and the 'bounce back' explanation of how the image is formed is misleading.
Part

. The task is to judge statements, so take the article apart and test each claim against the physics of MRI, then judge the article as a whole. Four claims are available to test: that MRI is based on the magnetic properties of atoms; that the field is roughly 10 000 times Earth's; that a very small percentage of hydrogen nuclei line up with it; and that the radio waves 'bounce back' from the lined-up atoms.

The first and third claims are correct: MRI detects the precession of the proton magnetic moment, and because the energies of the two spin states differ by only $h f \approx 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV}$ at body temperature, only a minute excess of nuclei occupies the aligned state - about 1 in $10^{7}$ - and that small excess is the whole signal. The second claim understates the field badly: a $1.5$ to $3\,\mathrm{T}$ clinical magnet is 30 000 to 60 000 times Earth's field. The fourth claim is the serious one: no radio wave is reflected back from the aligned nuclei. The radiofrequency pulse tips the magnetisation away from equilibrium and the signal is the radiation the relaxing, precessing nuclei emit; the signal strength is set by the spin density of the hydrogen and by the chemical environment (which is what gives T1 and T2 contrast), not by the number of nuclei a wave 'meets'.

content.text: Why is ultrasound imaging NOT used for investigating the function and structure of the brain?

Because the acoustic impedance of bone is very different from that of brain tissue. The fraction of intensity reflected at a boundary, $\left(\dfrac{Z_{2} - Z_{1}}{Z_{2} + Z_{1}}\right)^{2}$, rises sharply with the difference in impedance, so a large share of the incident intensity is reflected at each interface of the skull and only a small fraction is transmitted through to the brain, where it is further attenuated by the thickness and the density of the bone. Too little intensity therefore reaches the brain to form a useful image. The exception is the fontanel of an infant, where a membrane rather than bone separates the probe from the brain.

. Identify the property that blocks the ultrasound: the mismatch of acoustic impedance at each boundary, which converts most of the incident energy into reflected energy, leaving too little transmitted intensity to image the brain and adding the attenuation of the bone in between. The same relation used in part (a) supplies the justification.

Bone has an impedance of roughly $3.8 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ against about $1.5 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ for soft tissue, a large relative difference, so a substantial fraction is reflected at the skull surface and again at the inner surface, and the small transmitted fraction is attenuated in the several millimetres of bone. What reaches the brain carries too little energy to build an image, which is why CT, MRI or PET are used instead.

content.text: Assess the effects on the lives of individuals and the wider community of the production and use of X-rays, CAT scans and MRI.

Split the response into three clearly signposted sections: effects on the individual, effects on the wider community, then the judgement. The rubric assesses all three separately, so do not let one run into another.

Be specific about production as well as use. Saying how each image is made is worth a mark in its own right and shows the distinction between an X-ray photograph, a computed reconstruction and a magnetic resonance measurement.
Make the judgement explicit at the end and justify it against the two real negatives — cost and access, and ionising dose — rather than leaving it to be inferred.

All three allow non-invasive diagnosis of injuries and disease that would otherwise require surgery or be missed, greatly improving individual outcomes and saving lives; but they are expensive, so their use increases health costs and widens the gap in access between developed and developing communities, and the ionising radiation of X-rays and CT carries a small risk of causing cancer.

X-rays, CAT scans and MRI all produce images of internal structures without surgery, so they allow conditions such as fractures, tumours, internal bleeding and brain injury to be found early and treated. For individuals this means faster, less invasive treatment, less pain and faster recovery, and for many people it is lifesaving.

The effect on the wider community is also large: early diagnosis lowers the cost of treating advanced disease, allows screening programmes such as mammography to reduce mortality, and reduces the need for risky exploratory surgery.

However, the equipment is very expensive to buy, house and maintain and requires highly trained staff, so these technologies consume a large share of health budgets. In poorer countries and rural areas they are often unavailable, so the benefit is distributed unequally and the gap in health outcomes between rich and poor communities is widened.

X-rays and CAT scans use ionising radiation, which carries a small but real risk of inducing cancer in the patient, so scans are used only when the diagnostic benefit outweighs this risk, and MRI, which uses no ionising radiation, is preferred where it is equally suitable.

Judgement: the benefits to individual lives are very large and clearly outweigh the small radiation risk, but the cost and access issues mean that these technologies have increased inequality in health care as well as improved health outcomes.

content.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of CAT and PET scans in investigating the structure and function of the brain with reference to the images shown.
Image A: Dark areas show abnormal brain activity function.
Image B: White area shows the result of a stroke.
Osteoporosis is a degenerative disease in which there is a gradual loss of minerals in the bone. This leads to decreased bone strength and an increased chance of bone fractures.

Identify each image by what it is a record of: one shows where a substance has accumulated in the body, the other shows where the density of tissue differs from normal. The captions in the figures give the clue.
Then compare what each technique can see: one gives excellent anatomical detail but says nothing about function, the other shows function clearly but with poor anatomical detail.

For the second sub-part, use the same contrast idea as the rest of the question — matching the property of the radiation (or field) to the clinical question being asked — and make sure you say what each image actually tells the clinician to do next.

Image A is a PET scan and Image B is a CAT (CT) scan. PET - advantages: it maps function, showing which regions of the brain are metabolically active, so the abnormal activity appears as the dark areas of Image A and functional abnormality can be detected before any structural change is visible; it can be repeated to follow a course of treatment and it is the only one of the two that shows activity. Disadvantages: it needs an injected positron-emitting tracer, so the patient receives a dose of ionising radiation; it is expensive and slow; and its spatial resolution is poor, so the anatomy is not resolved. CAT - advantages: it shows structure in cross-section at millimetre resolution and is fast, relatively cheap and widely available, so the white area of the stroke in Image B is clearly delineated, its site and extent can be measured, and a haemorrhage can be distinguished from an infarct. Disadvantages: it uses X-rays, so it carries a small risk of inducing cancer and may require an injected contrast agent, and it gives no information about function. Comparison: CAT is used where structural damage is suspected and PET where a functional abnormality is being investigated, so the two are complementary and are often used together.
Part

. Identify each image from what it is a record of before comparing them. A grainy three-dimensional surface view with patches that are darker than the surrounding cortex, captioned as abnormal brain activity, is a nuclear-medicine image: the positron-emitting tracer has accumulated where the metabolism differs, so the dark areas are a map of function. An axial cross-section in which the skull is sharply outlined and one region is much brighter than the rest of the brain is a reconstructed X-ray image: brightness is X-ray attenuation, and the white area is the stroke. That makes Image A the PET scan and Image B the CAT scan.
Use the physics of each to explain what it shows and what it cannot show.

The two photons leave in opposite directions, so detecting them in coincidence in a ring of detectors localises each annihilation to the line joining the two detectors, and the set of such lines is back-projected into the image; where the tracer is taken up is where the dark areas are, and in the brain that follows glucose use and blood flow. The CAT image instead comes from attenuation of X-rays,

with the attenuation coefficient $\mu$ roughly proportional to the density and atomic number of the tissue. Scanning in many directions and reconstructing recovers $\mu$ in each voxel, so tissue that has died, bled or calcified differs from normal brain and appears as a bright or dark region whose position and size can be measured. The comparison for the answer therefore turns on two axes: CAT resolves structure and cannot resolve function, while PET resolves function and cannot resolve structure, and each carries a disadvantage (ionising radiation in both, but a radioactive tracer and poor resolution for PET, no functional information for CAT).
Part

content.text: With reference to the images shown, compare TWO imaging techniques which can be used to diagnose osteoporosis.

Any two suitable techniques may be compared; plain X-radiography and DEXA (dual energy X-ray absorptiometry) are the usual pair. Plain X-ray: a radiograph of the hip, spine or forearm is cheap, fast and available everywhere, and as bone loses mineral the cortex thins and the trabeculae become sparse, so the bone becomes more transparent on the image. Its disadvantage is that it is qualitative only: it shows loss of density only once it is substantial (typically more than 30 per cent), so it detects advanced osteoporosis and gives no numerical measure of bone strength and hence no prediction of fracture risk. DEXA: two X-ray beams of different wavelengths are passed through the hip or spine and the difference in absorption by bone and soft tissue gives an areal bone mineral density in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-2}}$ which is compared with the mean value for young adults, so that a T-score below $-2.5$ identifies osteoporosis. It is far more sensitive than plain radiography, so it detects and quantifies bone loss before fractures occur, and it is used to monitor treatment; its disadvantage is greater cost and complexity. Comparison: both techniques use X-rays and so both deliver a dose of ionising radiation, but DEXA gives a precise, quantitative, more sensitive measurement whereas plain radiography is cheap, simple and insensitive.

. The task is a comparison, so take each technique in the same order: how it works, what it shows, then why it does or does not detect the gradual loss of mineral. Quantitative against qualitative is the point of the comparison - a plain radiograph only becomes abnormal when a large fraction of the bone has been lost, whereas DEXA measures the areal density directly and compares it with a reference population, which is why it can quantify the disease and monitor treatment.

content.text: Describe how the existence of a binary star may be deduced.

A distance is never obtained from a brightness alone. Decide first whether the route is angular (an angle on the sky) or photometric (a comparison between apparent and absolute brightness), and write the corresponding relation before substituting.

For the angular route, a star with a smaller parallax is further away, and the scale of parallax for nearby stars is a few hundredths of an arcsecond, so a decimal point error changes the answer by a factor of ten.

For the photometric route, remember that magnitude is logarithmic and that the constant 5 comes from the definition of the parsec, so check the answer against the range of distances that is physically reasonable.

By two observations. Astrometry: the position of the star that appears single oscillates periodically about a fixed point in the sky instead of moving smoothly along a straight line, and that oscillation is the star's orbit about the common centre of mass, whose amplitude and period give the mass of the unseen companion. Spectroscopy: the absorption lines split into two sets that shift alternately towards the blue and towards the red, because the two stars move towards and then away from Earth as they orbit. Infrared or adaptive-optics imaging can also show the companion directly as a separate point of light at a small angular separation. The amplitude of the orbital motion is far too large to be due to a planet.
Part

. A binary shows itself as motion that a single star cannot produce, and the motion must be referred to the companion to earn the second mark. The key is to see that the observed motion is the sum of the motion of the whole system through space and the orbit of the star about the centre of mass, and that the same effect appears in the spectrum as a periodic Doppler shift of alternating sign.

content.text: The distance from the Sun to Earth is 1 astronomical unit (1 AU). The apparent magnitude of the Sun, when viewed from Earth, is $-26.5$. Calculate the apparent magnitude of the Sun when viewed from Saturn, a distance of 10 AU from the Sun.

$-21.5$. Saturn is 10 times further from the Sun than Earth, so by the inverse square law the intensity received is $1/10^{2} = 1/100$ of that seen from Earth, and $m_{2} - m_{1} = -2.5\log_{10}(I_{2}/I_{1}) = 5\log_{10}(d_{2}/d_{1}) = 5\log_{10}10 = 5$, giving $m_{2} = -26.5 + 5 = -21.5$.
. Two relations have to be combined. Brightness falls as the inverse square of the distance, and the magnitude scale is logarithmic, so a factor of 100 in intensity is 5 magnitudes, not 2.5.

Cross-check with the distance modulus: Saturn's mean distance of 10 AU is $4.85 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{pc}$, and with the Sun's absolute visual magnitude of $+4.7$ from the table in part (d), $m = 4.7 + 5\log_{10}(4.85 \times 10^{-6}) \approx -21.9$, which agrees to the precision of the rounded data. Note that a change of 2.5 magnitudes, which is what the import bundle recorded as $-24.0$, would correspond to a factor of 10 in intensity and is wrong; the factor is 100 because intensity falls as $1/d^{2}$.

content.text: Explain how TWO other characteristics or properties of a star can be deduced by observing the light received from the star.

Surface temperature: a hot star radiates more energy at short wavelengths, so a blue star is hotter than a red one. Measuring the intensity at several wavelengths and comparing the shape of the curve with black-body curves, or locating its peak and applying Wien's displacement law, gives the temperature numerically, and this is how the O, B, A, F, G, K and M spectral classes are assigned. Chemical composition: each element absorbs its own particular wavelengths, so the stellar spectrum is a continuous spectrum crossed by dark absorption lines; splitting the starlight with a prism or diffraction grating and matching those lines against laboratory spectra shows which elements are present, and the strength of a line indicates how abundant that element is. A third acceptable property is the star's motion: a shift of the lines towards the blue or the red gives the radial velocity by the Doppler effect, and a periodic variation of those shifts reveals a binary.

. Each property is deduced from a different feature of the light, and both the feature and the inference have to be named to earn the marks. For temperature the feature is the shape of the continuous spectrum and the inference is Wien's displacement law; for composition the feature is the pattern of dark absorption lines and the inference is the matching of those lines against laboratory spectra.

The link to the rest of the topic is that this is where the numbers in the table in part (d) come from: the spectral classes A0 to M2 are temperature classes, and the apparent and absolute magnitudes in that table are brightness measurements. content.text: Evaluate the ways that TWO technologies used in modern astrophysics have changed scientific understanding of celestial objects.
Give each technology its own paragraph and, in each, three things: what it is, how it works at the level of the physics, and the specific understanding it changed.
The rubric rewards a technology that overturned an accepted understanding. A technology that merely produced a better image does not score as highly, so choose two that changed what we believed.
End with an evaluation rather than a summary, and make the judgement about how scientific understanding changed, not about whether the technology is good.

Spectroscopy and radio telescopes have both transformed our understanding: spectroscopy revealed the composition, temperature and motion of stars and proved that stars are made of the same elements as Earth, while radio astronomy revealed cold hydrogen, molecules and the background radiation from which the expansion of the universe and the Big Bang were discovered.

Technology 1 - spectroscopy: a prism or diffraction grating spreads starlight into a spectrum. Kirchhoff's laws allow the dark absorption lines to be identified with particular elements, so before 1859 the composition of the stars was unknown. Spectroscopy then showed that the Sun contains the same elements as the Earth, so astronomy became a branch of physics and the idea that the heavens were made of a different, perfect substance was abandoned. Measurement of the displacement of the lines by the Doppler effect later gave the radial velocities of stars and, through Hubble's law, the expansion of the universe.

Technology 2 - radio telescopes: detectors operating at radio wavelengths, using dishes of increasing size and interferometry to achieve great angular resolution, revealed radio emission from cold hydrogen at 21 cm, the molecular gas in star-forming regions, pulsars, quasars and the cosmic microwave background. The existence of the cosmic microwave background was decisive evidence for the Big Bang, and the mapping of its tiny variations by COBE and WMAP has changed our understanding of how the large-scale structure of the universe formed.

Judgement: both technologies extended astronomy beyond the visible spectrum and turned it from a qualitative into a quantitative, evidence-based science, and both produced results (stellar composition, the expansion, the Big Bang) that overturned accepted scientific understandings.
A weaker response would be one that simply listed technologies without linking them to a specific change in scientific understanding.
